# What the deeper record clarifies

Selected public procedural and institutional records, checked as of October 17, 2026. The evidence supports a more precise chronology, while leaving the full file inventory and several implementation steps unresolved. Official hosting, original authorship and factual verification are distinguished throughout.

## The early deal has several dates, not one

The inspected Supreme Court appendix reproduces an agreement signed by Epstein on September 24, 2007 and by a federal prosecutor on September 27. The reproduced addendum has separate October 29 and October 30 signature dates. These are party-filed reproductions on an official court website; they do not independently authenticate the originating counterparts or establish an effective date. The later OPR executive summary dates the state plea to June 30, 2008 and describes the imposed sentence. It does not establish time actually served. [Agreement and judgment appendix, selected pages 56–75](https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/24/24-1073/355252/20250424150144637_24-__PetitionForWritOfCertiorari.pdf); [OPR executive summary, pages 1–3](https://www.justice.gov/opr/page/file/1336471/download).

## The 2019 criminal case ended without a verdict

The prosecutor’s case-status page separates the August 19 dismissal request, the August 27 hearing at which decision was reserved, and the August 29 entry of a nolle prosequi order. The original dismissal order was not obtained. This source-qualified closure is not an acquittal, exoneration or adjudication of the charged allegations. [SDNY case-status chronology, August 2019 entries](https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/programs/victim-witness-services/united-states-v-jeffrey-epstein-19-cr-490-rmb).

## Maxwell’s criminal stages remain distinct

The sentencing announcement dates June 28, 2022, while the reproduced judgment and appellate opinion identify June 29. The inspected judgment reproduction records five guilty-verdict counts but judgment on three counts; the two other guilty counts were treated as multiplicitous. The imposed terms run concurrently, rather than adding into a longer total. The appellate opinion affirmed the June 29 judgment on September 17, 2024; the rehearing order is dated November 25. The Supreme Court docket separates the April 10, 2025 petition filing from April 14 docketing and records certiorari denied on October 6. That denial is not a new merits determination. A later order dated January 21, 2026 describes a section 2255 collateral petition filed December 17, 2025 as outstanding at that time. The original petition and its later status were not inspected. [January 2026 order, pages 3–4](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2026-01/Maxwell%2020cr330%20-%20Opinion%20%26%20Order%201.21.26.pdf). [Judgment reproduction, PDF pages 69–75](https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/24/24-1073/355252/20250424150144637_24-__PetitionForWritOfCertiorari.pdf); [Second Circuit opinion, pages 1–2](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-ca2-22-01426/pdf/USCOURTS-ca2-22-01426-0.pdf); [Rehearing order, PDF page 27](https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/24/24-1073/337362/20250117133905126_22-1426.pdf); [Supreme Court docket 24-1073](https://www.supremecourt.gov/docket/docketfiles/html/public/24-1073.html).

## An unsealing order is one step in a publication chain

The 2019 civil opinion makes summary-judgment unsealing contingent on issuance of the appellate mandate and remands other materials for individualized review. The January 3, 2024 district order describes a prior fourteen-day stay and says the parties planned to begin filing later that day, except for two reserved matters. No appellate mandate, original district implementing order from the 2019 sequence, original December 18, 2023 order, completed-filing receipt or complete released-document list was obtained. Those records support conditional authority and a reported plan, not a verified complete publication event. [Appellate opinion, pages 13–14 and 24–25](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-ca2-18-02868/pdf/USCOURTS-ca2-18-02868-0.pdf); [January 2024 district order, pages 1–2](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2024-01/15cv7433%2001032023%20115pm%20%281%29.pdf).

## Later release authority carries category-specific safeguards

Two original Maxwell-case orders distinguish the August 11, 2025 denial from the December 9 Act-based authorization. The later order permits Maxwell grand-jury disclosure with privacy protections and modifies the criminal discovery protective order. Before covered discovery is released, it requires a personal sworn certification by the SDNY United States Attorney; that certification requirement does not apply to every DOJ-held record. This review did not verify a filed certification, fulfillment of its conditions or actual publication. The January process letter’s separate civil-sealed and corrections-officer grand-jury categories were not linked to original motions or later dispositions. [August opinion, pages 1, 11 and 31](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-08/20cr330%20Opinion%20%26%20Order%208.11.25-1.pdf); [December opinion, pages 23–24](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/PAE%20Maxwell%20Opinion%202025.12.09%20%28As%20Docketed%29.pdf); [January process letter, pages 5–6](https://www.justice.gov/opa/media/1426091/dl#page=1).

## Court supervision and agency reporting have separate limits

The January 21, 2026 Maxwell order denies a proposed amicus intervention to supervise DOJ’s compliance with the disclosure statute. It explains that modifying the discovery protective order removed an obstacle to statutory disclosure; that earlier modification did not itself order DOJ to release records or grant broad supervisory jurisdiction. The denial is without prejudice to a separate lawsuit, and the court did not decide the standing or private-cause-of-action arguments. This is a ruling about the requested procedural route, not a finding that DOJ complied with the disclosure law. [January order, pages 3–7](https://www.nysd.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2026-01/Maxwell%2020cr330%20-%20Opinion%20%26%20Order%201.21.26.pdf).

The Federal Register’s August 27, 2026 issue publishes a notice dated August 21 and a reproduced DOJ Section 3 report dated February 14. The notice says the report was submitted to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees. The record establishes this official publication event, but no separate congressional receipt was inspected. DOJ’s descriptions of release and withholding remain the agency’s assertions, not independently verified completeness. No first-disclosure date for the report or document-level release inventory is inferred. [Published notice and report, PDF pages 1–4](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-27/pdf/2026-17533.pdf).

## Financial records describe different legal and accounting stages

The original NYDFS consent order imposes a $150 million penalty across several compliance matters, including Epstein-related banking and foreign-bank correspondent relationships. It provides no Epstein-only allocation. Its extracted counterpart text indicates July 6, 2020, with signature placement visually unverified. The order credits cooperation and remediation alongside its adverse regulatory findings. No later payment or compliance completion was established. [NYDFS consent order, pages 31–38](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2020/07/ea20200706_deutsche_bank_consent_order.pdf).

USVI DOJ’s September 26, 2023 announcement describes a $75 million JPMorgan settlement, including a $10 million designated use within that total. The estate announcement has a November 30, 2022 release date and December 1 posting label; it describes $105 million cash, half of Little St. James sale proceeds, a separate $450,000 remediation commitment and nonmonetary undertakings. These are official party accounts of commitments. The original agreements, precise corporate obligor for the bank, execution dates and settlement-specific performance records remain unverified. The estate announcement’s more-than-$80 million tax-benefit description is not an additional amount to sum with $105 million. [JPMorgan announcement](https://usvidoj.com/usvi-doj-achieves-historic-75-million-victim-supporting-settlement-with-jpmorganchase/); [estate announcement](https://usvidoj.com/u-s-virgin-islands-attorney-general-settles-sex-trafficking-case-against-estate-of-jeffrey-epstein-and-co-defendants-for-over-105-million/).

A BDO report dated January 27, 2026 says the government received approximately $97 million during fiscal 2023 under estate-related settlement agreements. It does not itemize that population by payer or obligation. Subtracting it from an announced settlement total would manufacture an unsupported unpaid balance. The audit also describes funds not established and a management implementation target of fiscal 2026; the exact observation date and subsequent completion were not established in that round. Its audit-scope qualifications and limited treatment of management’s response remain important. [Audit, printed pages 1–4 and 60–61](https://dof.vi.gov/sites/default/files/docs/GVI%20Yellow%20Book%202023.pdf).

## A fund law is now traceable; actual fund administration remains a separate question

An Act 8920 copy hosted by the Virgin Islands Port Authority contains the legislative text, executive objections and a later override certificate. It records passage on September 27, 2024 and governor approval of the fund-establishment and cultural-center provisions on October 10. The October 16 override concerns four other specified sections; it is not assigned as the enactment date of every provision. Sections 1 and 2 establish distinct Treasury funds and reporting duties. Section 7 appropriates $10 million to VIPA for a St. John cultural center. This is statutory authority and appropriation, not an inspected account setup, transfer or completed project. The copy is not a verified current consolidated law. [Act copy, PDF pages 1, 3–5 and 8–9](https://www.viport.com/_files/ugd/e0a2e7_7804b494a53949d58fff897b3575cf50.pdf).

VIPA board-nominee testimony dated February 18, 2026 says the cultural-center funds had not yet been received. It separately describes earlier design funding as received and expended. This is attributed testimony at a historical document date, not a current treasury reconciliation. Its reference to the “36th Legislature” differs from the Act copy’s “35th”; the difference remains unresolved. Legal creation, administrative establishment, appropriation, receipt and project delivery must remain separate. [Testimony, PDF page 5, printed page 4](https://legvi.org/committeemeetings/Rules%20And%20Judiciary/February%2026%2C%202026/Nominees/Ms.%20Leona%20Smith/Testimony%20-%20Leona%20V%20Smith%20VIPA%20Board%2018%20Feb%202026%20-%20final.pdf).

## Questions that remain open

- Which originating agreement counterparts and state judgment establish execution, entry and case-number linkage?
- What do the original 2019 dismissal and hearing orders say, including the unresolved year printed in a later judicial reference?
- What are Maxwell’s originating judgment stamps, amendments and mandate dates, and the later disposition of the collateral petition described in January 2026?
- Which civil documents were actually filed, on what dates, under which operative orders and exceptions?
- Was the required discovery certification filed, what did it cover, and which records were actually published? What happened to the two separate categories described in the January letter?
- What do the original USVI settlement agreements and court dispositions establish? Which beneficiary-free treasury ledgers, required fund reports and dated compliance records reconcile obligations, receipts and implementation? The Act copy supplies statutory authority, but not those accounting records.
- Is there a document-level release/change inventory that can establish overlaps, moved files or historical changes? Current labels, official reporting and announced page totals alone cannot do that. No residual “missing page” total can be calculated from overlapping populations.

These gaps are acquisition and verification limits. They do not establish concealment, guilt by association or an unexplained loss of money. Five bounded rounds deepen the record; they do not make it a complete corpus.
